title: The C Programming Language
description: The book that teaches C and, by extension, how a computer actually executes code. Read it twice — once for syntax, once for the model it gives you.

title: Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs
description: The classic text on building abstraction layers. Demanding, and worth every hour. The full text is free online.

title: Composing Programs
description: A modern, web-native adaptation of SICP with Python. The club's entry point for first-years who want the SICP mindset without the Scheme.

title: The Missing Semester of Your CS Education
description: MIT's crash course in the tools every student is assumed to know but nobody teaches: shell, editors, git, debugging, data wrangling.

title: git-for-beginners (official docs)
description: Start with the Pro Git book's first three chapters, then use the reference. Skip the ten-minute videos.

title: The Art of Command Line
description: A dense, single-file field guide to the command line. Read one page a day and try everything it mentions.

title: Linux Journey
description: A structured path through Linux basics: the filesystem, users, permissions, processes, and networking, with practice pages.

title: The Linux Command Line
description: A free, thorough book that turns you from a clicker into someone who composes commands. Our first-year recommended reading.

title: man pages you should know
description: Why `apropos` and `man -k` are your first debugging tools. Learning to read documentation beats memorizing it.

title: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces
description: The canonical free OS text: virtualization, concurrency, persistence — with projects that mirror what our systems group builds.

title: Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective
description: CS:APP connects C, assembly, the memory hierarchy, and links/loading into one coherent picture. The lab assignments are legendary.

title: Systems Performance
description: How to measure systems before theorizing about them. Reaches for when you want to understand why things are slow, not just that they are.

title: MDN Web Docs
description: The only web reference we recommend. If a web answer isn't from MDN, verify it against MDN before trusting it.

title: Web Browser Engineering
description: Build a tiny web browser from first principles in 400 pages. The best cure for 'magic black box' thinking about the web.

title: CSS for Engineers
description: Layout as an engineering problem: box model, flow, flexbox, grid, and why 'make it work' comes before 'make it pretty'.

title: Practical Deep Learning for Coders
description: fast.ai's top-down course: train real models in lesson one, then fill in theory. We run this inside our AI reading group.

title: Neural Networks and Deep Learning
description: Michael Nielsen's free, interactive book. The chapter on how backpropagation actually works is the best one we know.

title: Hugging Face NLP Course
description: From tokenizers to fine-tuning, hands-on. The companion to our Nodhini project.

title: PortSwigger Web Security Academy
description: Free labs that teach web vulnerabilities by making you exploit them. The best practical security training that exists for free.

title: OverTheWire Bandit
description: A level-based game that teaches Linux security basics through puzzles. Our CTF team's warm-up.

title: CryptoPals
description: Cryptography challenges that force you to implement attacks, not memorize them. Expect to feel humbled.

title: The Algorithm Design Manual
description: Skiena's practical take on algorithm design — a catalog of problems and when to reach for them, instead of a wall of proofs.

title: CSES Problem Set
description: 300 curated problems ranked by difficulty. Our algorithms group's homework source.

title: VisuAlgo
description: Interactive algorithm visualization. Pair it with our own AlgoPlay and you will never need a gif again.

title: The Art of Electronics
description: The engineer's handbook for circuits. Keep it next to VoltLab's bench; answer 'why is it doing that?' before touching the firmware.

title: ESP32 Technical Reference
description: The datasheet-ish manual for our datalogger board. Learning to read reference manuals is a skill; start here.

title: Practical Electronics for Inventors
description: A gentler entry than Horowitz & Hill, with the same honesty about how components actually behave.

title: How to Contribute to Open Source
description: Open Source Guide's checklist for a first contribution, from reading CONTRIBUTING to surviving your first review.

title: Choosing a License
description: What MIT, Apache-2.0, and GPL actually mean for your project. Read this before the club's next release.

title: Semantic Versioning
description: The spec our projects follow. Version numbers are communication; learn to speak it.
